problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi .$
worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,\pi \end{aligned}
$$
